title: A Week In Long Island, NY On A $210,000 Joint Income
text:
A Week In Long Island, NY On A $210,000 Joint Income

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: A stay-at-home parent who makes $0 per year and spends it on some Kala Namak (black salt).

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

This diary was written in 2026.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Stay-at-home parent
Age: 38
Location: Long Island, NY
Salary: $0
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My husband E.’s salary is $210,000 plus a bonus target of $40,000. We share our finances in a joint bank and credit accounts. Additionally, we’ll make $30K this year from a trust in E.’s name (amount varies year to year).
Assets:
Investment accounts: $894K plus $65K earmarked for our children.
Debt: $795,000 (house); $381,550 (condo)
Paycheck Amount (bi-weekly): $5,000
Pronouns: She/her

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs: $7,530.38
Loan Payments:
Car lease: $650
401k: $1,800
Utilities: ~$200
Phone plan: $25 (one of us is gifted a family plan)
Internet: $79.99
YouTube Premium: $23
Disney+: $4.99
Sirius Satellite Radio: $7.27
Apple Music: $10.99
IVF embryo storage: $115

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
No. I was in foster care, so all my caretaker cared about was getting the monthly check that came in for housing me. I participated in college because all my peers were going, and it seemed like a logical next step since I knew I could get a lot of financial aid and I’d have a place to live. I ended up getting a mix of needs-based and merit-based aid, so I didn’t have any loans (I was extremely lucky) for undergrad. I went to graduate school and didn’t get any aid. I took out modest loans at okay interest rates and paid them off aggressively over a few years.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
I was raised by a single mom (before my siblings and I were placed in foster care as teenagers). She talked to my siblings and me like we were adults. She stressed about money all the time. Our vacations were infrequent and done on the cheap. We camped in tents at a campsite and cooked all our own food. I once saw a paper she’d been writing on; it was a ledger for a vacation we were taking from New York to New Jersey. She’d written down every planned expense before the trip, including car mileage and gas cost to the gallon. My mom didn’t educate us about finances because she wasn’t good at it. I speculate, or maybe she was waiting until we got older, but then we were taken away from her. She lived (and still does live) paycheck to paycheck. Though she no longer takes care of dependents and now earns a comfortable, liveable wage, she is still unable to budget well or plan ahead.

What was your first job and why did you get it?
My mom was a waitress and would bring me to work with her (I was elementary school age). It was my first unpaid job, but a job I took seriously as it was my first ever! I was given the task of filling the dishwasher with soap and running it. There were two bottles of soap next to each other and I was to ask the guy towering above next to me if I couldn’t remember which to use. Eventually I got embarrassed of not being able to remember which it was, so I guessed. I guessed wrong and after a minute, the floor filled with soap suds. The guy yelled a lot and kicked me out of the kitchen, never to return again. After that, I sat in one of the booths and played with my paper dolls. If I was lucky, my mom would give me some money to get a new paper doll book, and I would run to the Barnes & Noble (or was it Borders Books?) and get a new one or sit in the aisles and play with stuff.

For my first paid job, I was a paper girl for a newspaper in middle school (so around 12 to 14 years old). I had a scooter, which I balanced the papers on either side of the handles, so I used that to throw the papers to the neighbours and then race home to get my stuff to go to school. Before going out, we had to either package them with rubber bands or plastic sleeves in the event of rain or snow. I can’t remember if both of my sisters did the job too or only one of them. Weekly, I’d go after school to collect payment for the subscriptions and my take-home pay was any tips I received. I got the job for spending money. I used it to buy candy, toys, and clothing that wasn’t hand–me–downs. And I bought my first cell phone, which was a flip phone that I loaded a few dollars on a phone card. The only game I remember playing on the thing was Snake.

Did you worry about money growing up?
I worried about money growing up because of the things our biological mom shared with us before we were taken away from her. Stressing about making payments, utility shut-off, and moving happened a lot. Taking a cold shower in a cold house was not fun.

Do you worry about money now?
I still worry about money now despite a decent nest egg and marketable skills, so I don’t think it will ever go away. It’s not something I have been able to logic myself out of, unfortunately.

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
I became financially responsible for myself when I aged out of foster care. I had extended care (since I was in college) and finished college at age 21, so the agency, at the time, gave me a small amount of cash (I think $600?), furniture you could pick from a catalog (I got a futon, a coffee table, and a TV stand), and helps you to secure housing. I was lucky enough to have the Section 8 program when I aged out and eventually earned too much money to warrant support. That benefit was a lifesaver. I would have been homeless when I left college had the housing transition program not been in place. I have been a long-time Money Diary reader, and have always been fascinated by people’s financial safety net responses. I would say that I never had a person I could financially rely upon before marriage. My safety net was my credit cards. I did use them and get into debt when I had to, and luckily have not had to go into severe credit card debt more than once. Now that I’m married, if we ever needed it, E.’s parents would be a financial safety net. However, like many loans received from family and friends, it would come with strings attached, so we wouldn’t consider it an option unless something dire happened.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
No.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Tuesday

7 a.m. — My husband, E., heads to a spin class. I keep shoving a pacifier and formula bottle in our baby T.’s mouth (E. always moves him into bed with me in the morning, so I can sleep a bit more). I give up on sleep and go to brush my teeth. I then wash my face using Cetaphil, followed by The Inkey List Peptide Moisturizer and some Kiehl’s eye cream. I keep it simple per my dermatologist.

8:30 a.m. — I feed our cat. E. already fed our dog. I go downstairs to make breakfast. I ask Siri to play “Banana Pancakes” by Jack Johnson. It makes for a nice, easy morning playlist. I sauté spinach and sliced white mushrooms with oil, garlic, and salt. I make a tofu scramble from a random recipe online. E. rates it 4 out of 5. The spinach is so yummy! T. starts crying, so E. takes him to go change his diaper.

9:30 a.m. — I cuddle with T. in bed. He passes out quickly but I can’t so I read an article in The Atlantic. I grab a lemon meringue Coconut Cult and do a crossword puzzle. I’m still hungry so I grab a handful of peanut butter pretzels and a can of club soda, and settle in to work on a book I’ve been writing. Researching, learning new things, outlining my words and illustrations — this has been making me happy with this little project of mine.

12:15 p.m. — I take a break from writing to have lunch. I have a bowl of It-Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad from Bon Appetit that I prepped a few days ago. The Little Man (who was at his grandparents’ place) was dropped off by grandpa earlier and just woke up from his morning nap. I give him a peanut butter and jelly Uncrustable, which he demolishes, and some milk. He crawls into his stroller so I guess he wants a walk. E. gets the baby prepped and I get our Little Man ready for a walk out in the snow. After our walk I put on Bluey for the Little Man and work on my book some more.

5 p.m. — E. feeds the Little Man mush overnight oats for dinner. E. makes us ravioli with a butternut squash sauce and a side of sautéed kale for dinner. I put on Wayne’s World because I’ve been wanting to rewatch it and I like the soundtrack. We haven’t watched much TV lately as a couple because there hasn’t been anything we’ve both wanted to watch. T. is sleeping on top of me so I can’t move anyway. I feed T. a bottle when he wakes. We have dinner; I have a glass of red wine with it.

7:00 p.m. — E. takes the Little Man up for bath time and bed. I feed T. a bottle while finishing the movie. I journal a few sentences. Feed cat.

9:00 p.m. — Bedtime.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Wednesday

7 a.m. — T. wakes me. I stick a bottle in his mouth, he downs it and falls back asleep. I try to fall back asleep, too. T. starts to stretch and kick a lot so I pull out his piano kick gym. It’s the only interactive toy he can play with at his age. He starts kicking the piano and smiling.

7:30 a.m. — I put together a bowl of corn pop cereal and ask E. to make me a coffee because I think it always tastes better when someone else makes it. It’s a cup of hot Folgers with cold foam (maple flavored) from Trader Joe’s on top. I eat cereal in bed and watch T. play with his toy. He is adorable. E. goes to get our nanny in our car from the train station! She’s with us three days a week for 10 hours a day, generally.

8 a.m. — I put Bluey on projected to the bedroom wall for the Little Man to watch. I hand off T. to the nanny and the Little Man and I go to his room and take a glorious nap together.

12 p.m. — The Little Man wakes. I feed him a mush overnight oat and heat up leftover potatoes and tofu scramble for myself. E. helps himself to lentil salad from the fridge and goes back to his office area for some meetings. I didn’t have Indian black salt, as per the recipe, for the tofu scramble and hadn’t heard of it before. The scramble came out fine without it but the reviews on Amazon rave about its umami flavor. I’m influenced. $6.99

5 p.m. — E. goes to the grocery store to grab a few things for dinner: Cucumber, cherry tomato, olives, onion, and bananas. He also picks up a few things from the pharmacy (I think that one is personal haha). $23.50

6 p.m. — I prep dinner for everyone: A pita bread open-face sandwich with hummus, cucumber, tomato, feta, dill, olives, and lemon juice. As I’m eating it, I remember I planned on putting sumac on it. Oh well. I relieve our nanny so she can eat before she needs to leave.

7 p.m. — I put Little Man to bed. He decides to play on the floor and falls asleep with his stuffed dog as his pillow on the floor surrounded by his toys. This kid can fall asleep anywhere and I’m jealous.

9 p.m. — I feed the cat and wash my face and brush my teeth. I get in bed and scroll Reddit before lights out.

Daily Total: $30.39

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Thursday

4:30 a.m. — The Little Man is up and won’t go back to sleep. I join him in his room while he goes between playing, babbling, and crying. E. stays with T. in our room, who is up periodically for feedings. I eventually go downstairs and make a bowl of Corn Pops and share them with the Little Man.

9 a.m. — E. picks up our nanny. The Little Man is napping and E. and I leave to take T. to a doctor’s appointment. I prep a thermos of coffee to take with me. T. was transverse [the baby is lying horizontally] when I was pregnant with him, so they want to look at his hips and make sure everything is okay.

11 a.m. — E. and I are both so hungry so we stop off for some food near the doctor’s. We’ve been to this sandwich place before and it’s so yummy. I get a tuna melt, E. gets a chicken panini and a Diet Coke, and then we get a homemade chocolate chip cookie to share. The cookie is stuffed with a rainbow cookie inside. It’s so extra and yum. I make note of the brand and its website because I think it would make a good gift for friends and neighbors ($36.27). We stop at Whole Foods and Saks off Fifth. I saw online that they were going out of business but there aren’t any sales and there’s a ton of inventory. We get lime, tuna steaks, pasta, pasta sauce, some Rao’s prepared soups, and dark chocolate peppermint cremes ($70.87). $107.14

2 p.m. — I interview for a new job. It goes okay.

3 p.m — I do a Caroline Girvan workout on YouTube from her Iron Series. I learned about her from a fellow Money Diary writer and I like her workouts even more than all the ones on Beach Body. I find hers to be tough but I can still get through them.

3:30 p.m. — I realize we are out of Everything But The Bagel Sesame Seasoning, which I need to make dinner, so I drive to Trader Joe’s. I get some chicken, bean rice and cheese burritos, the lemon arugula lazy salad I love so much, pumpkin seeds, truffle marcona almonds, delice cheese to go with the almonds, Everything But The Bagel Sesame Seasoning, snack bites, and a fruit strip. E. feeds Little Man dinner while I’m gone. Overnight oats, tofu eggs, and sugar snap peas. At this age, he’s eating everything — even weird combos like this. We are lucky. $56.87

5 p.m. — I make everything crusted tuna steaks and a side of snap peas. I follow the recipe from What To Cook When You Don’t Feel Like Cooking by Caroline Chambers, which I borrowed from the library’s Libby app. I rate my execution 4 out of 5. The snap peas are so yummy coated in sesame oil and leftover seasoning from the tuna in the pan. I house a few Reese’s Oreos for dessert.

7 p.m. — I put the Little Man down for bed with a bottle of milk. E. takes our nanny to the train station and goes to a spin class. I pick up the book I Regret Almost Everything by Keith McNally to read. I got it as a birthday gift and have been itching to read it. I love reading food books and memoirs. So far, this one is more of the latter.

8 p.m. — I take a break to go on the Trader Joe’s website and submit a form about a discontinued product. I haven’t seen the Meatless Meatballs lately and I miss them so. I like theirs better than the competitor brands. The form I fill out probably won’t have any impact but one can dream.

Daily Total: $164.01

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Friday

6:30 a.m. — The Little Man wakes. (At some point during the night, I went to sleep in his room because he was crying).

7 a.m — We go downstairs for breakfast. I have a lemon meringue Coconut Cult and sprinkle in mini chocolate chips. The Little Man doesn’t like it so I sprinkle Cheerios and banana pieces on the highchair. I’m going to the city today to meet my sister at her college dorm and celebrate her birthday. We are going to QCNY spa. They have a birthday promotion where the birthday person gets free entry in the month of their birth with a paying customer, but I waited to get a ticket too long and the birthday promo tickets were all claimed for the times we were able to go, so I bought both tickets at full price.

7:30 a.m. — I make some coffee and bring it to E. in bed as a little treat. E. and T. are just hanging out in bed, scrolling the internet.

9:30 a.m. — I grab a Nature Valley Peanut Butter granola bar and we take the Little Man to the library for baby sign language, but he’s not having it today. He’s rubbing his eyes and whining so we leave early and E. takes him home for nap time. I walk to the train station, which is near the library, and catch the train to the city. I read my book on the commute. $11.25

11 a.m. — I stop in at Milk Bar to get my sister some red velvet cake truffles to toss in her birthday gift bag because she’s been into red velvet lately. I get an iced cereal milk latte (it’s so yum) and a triple peanut butter cookie. The cookie is just okay. I put half away for later because I want to eat something more substantial ($18.61). I stop at Black Seed Bagels since I pass by it and get bagels and orange juice for me and my sister ($19.11). I stop at Eataly to get a Marvis toothpaste to add to her gift bag, too. She always sneaks into my bathroom when she comes to our home to use my toothpaste because she loves it. I get one for myself too since I’m running low ($22.86). Before this week, I purchased some other things that are in her gift bag (a Dutch oven and flaky sea salt because she’s recently gotten into cooking, a dry brush and reusable cotton rounds for makeup and nail polish removal). $60.58

1 p.m. — We get to the spa and have fun in the saunas and pools. Staff give us various complimentary treats such as cookies and face masks. We use a bunch of lotions and scrubs in different rooms. Our skin looks so good when we happen to see a mirror to glance in! We take a break to have a snack and drinks at the cafe. We each get a margarita, a snack plate to share with cheese, crackers and vegetables, and a prosecco strawberry sorbet. We stay in the outdoor infinity pool that overlooks lower Manhattan to watch the sunset. $401.62

7 p.m. — E. is early into the city, so he grabs a drink before dinner at a dive bar ($9). $9

8 p.m. — We meet E. for dinner. The table isn’t ready, so they comp us drinks at the bar and then a bunch of appetizers when we finally sit down. They apologize too many times for the table being ready so late. We eat and decline dessert. They bring us a complimentary dessert anyway for my sister’s birthday with a candle and she’s so smiley. It comes to $259.00 but I get a $50 American Express Gold Card benefit, so $209.00 it is! $209.00

10 p.m. — We decide to go to a cocktail bar. E. and my sister do several rounds of lemon drop shots. I sip two cocktails slowly… my stomach hurts and I know if I get drunk I’m going to throw up, and I already somehow feel like crap, so I don’t drink much. My sister keeps trying to pay for a round but E. keeps paying. Finally, my sister gets the bill first at the last round and has flirty banter with the waiter. I don’t know if she actually wanted to pay the whole time or get this guy’s attention. She excitedly tells me he flirted back. I tell her they always flirt back with her, and she graciously says “no, not always.” $154.32

12 a.m. — We walk my sister back to her dorm. Her life plan is to go to her old job where she was a dancer and reconnect with a bartender who was in love with her. I tell her not to break his heart this time and to be safe. E. and I get on the train to go home. For fun, we look up a cab, and it’s $175. A hotel in Manhattan for the night, comparatively, is $95. Either way, we get on the train like reasonable people who spent a ton on food and drinks tonight and go home. E. falls asleep on the train and I’m engrossed in my book. E. tries to initiate sex at home and we have a talk. I have no sex drive after giving birth for the second time. I’m worried it won’t return ever and he will give up and divorce me eventually. He says that won’t happen. Do they have Viagra for women??? $22.50

Daily Total: $868.27

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Saturday

11 a.m. — I lay in bed until 11. It’s pretty glorious. I keep waking and then putting myself back to sleep. I hear T. cry periodically. The nanny slept over so we could have the night out last night, and she’s still taking care of the baby. I go downstairs and make a bowl of Corn Pops.

12 p.m. — E. takes our nanny to the train station ($900 plus dinner for date night ($39.35)). $939.35

12 p.m. — The weather is so nice out, sunny and in the 50s, so E. wants to walk to a local restaurant with T. in the stroller before the grandparents bring the Little Man home from his sleepover. We get loaded nachos, club soda and iced coffee and feed T. a bottle while we eat. We walk the long way home because it’s so nice out. T. falls asleep on top of me while I read my book. I fall asleep, too. $32.13

6 p.m. — I make lentil burgers from a Bon Appétit recipe. I add egg as a binder, as I don’t know how this recipe works without it. E. feeds the Little Man some mac and cheese, and T. gets a bottle.

7 p.m. — After we eat, I bathe the Little Man and put him to bed. I read my book and have some dark chocolate peppermint creams.

10 p.m. — I have a banana and a Babybel snack. Brush teeth, floss, wash face. Give the pillow some head.

Daily Total: $971.48

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Sunday

8:30 a.m. — I lay in bed with T. 8:30. I kept him asleep with bottles and pacifiers. I make tofu scramble again because this time I can try it with the black salt that came in the mail. It’s crazy how eggy it smells. E. added cold cheese on top last time, so I fold in some shredded mozzarella. I would prefer cheddar but the mozzarella is already pre-shredded. The flavor isn’t that much different with black salt. The Little Man goes down for his morning nap.

10:30 a.m. — E. goes to spin and I feed T. a bottle and read my book. He falls asleep on me but not for long. I try to hold in a cough and can’t, which wakes him.

1:00 p.m. — I feed the Little Man an Uncrustable for lunch and pack everyone up to go to E.’s godparent’s house for bagels and a hike. We forgot to take the harness for T., so I take a nap on the couch. E.’s godmother takes T., and E. goes for a hike with the Little Man and his godfather.

5 p.m. — We go to E.’s parents’ house for dinner. We order Greek food for pickup. E.’s parents pay.

8 p.m. — We arrive home and our Target grocery delivery arrived on our doorstep. We ordered a bunch of produce, some snacks, Aquaphor, and baby socks. We put the food away and the kids to bed. I put the dishes away and load the dishwasher because we need bottles for the night. I do a crossword and pass out. $102.80

Daily Total: $102.80

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Monday

6 a.m. — The kids wake us up. E. takes the Little Man with him to the car shop to trade in our car for a loaner while ours gets repaired. I’m texting my father-in-law about politics and he isn’t answering me. It’s kinda early in the morning but you know how people get about politics??? Lol. I can’t stand the silence anymore so I call my father-in-law’s best friend. I know he screens his calls so he won’t answer but he will call me back at ungodly times of day, so I wait. I also pepper my sister with memes.

8 a.m. — Why isn’t anyone answering me? It’s like 8 a.m. now, which seems like an acceptable time for communication, and my brother-in-law isn’t answering me either. Where is everyone? Did the apocalypse finally happen? Oh wait, I look at my chat — jeez, I messaged a lot of people this morning. One person did respond to a birthday message I sent.

8:30 a.m. — I tidy up the house and E. comes home for the car repair shop with a frappe from Brew Crew for me — sweet! I read a bit while taking care of T., and grandpa comes over to relieve me and spend time with T. I chat on the phone for a while with an old neighbor who is a mom now as well, so we chat about kids, family, and career struggles as moms. I spend some time applying for jobs. $7.44

2 p.m. — I take the Little Man to a dance class at the library ($5), and E. and T. go to trade the loaner car back for our car. $5

2:30 p.m. — We’re told the total damage for a broken sensor issue we’ve been itching to fix: $634.38.

3 p.m. — E. goes to spin class and picks up some odds and ends for meals coming up (lime, lemon, etc). I prep a salad lunch for the next few days and make a shwarma spice mix to have on hand for potatoes (inspired by our dinner out the other night) and watch T. The Little Man took a nap right after his class; he doesn’t often do an afternoon nap. $3

5:30 p.m. — I whip together Crispy Miso Lime Tofu from the cookbook I took out from the library. It comes together in like 15 minutes and then I make a side of quick cooking garlic and herb rice. I rate the recipe 5/5. The Little Man won’t eat anything, so we don’t force it and let him have milk. I clean up and make a dessert from the same cookbook; it’s a chocolate peanut butter cup pudding type thing. It’s another quick recipe to make but has to chill in the fridge for hours to set. E. goes upstairs to put T. to bed and I tidy while the Little Man stays up late because of his nap schedule, watching Bluey.

7:00 p.m. — I take a bath with the Little Man and then put him to bed. He wakes, and E. goes to lie with him. I tidy up the downstairs and settle in with a book for the night.

Daily Total: $649.82

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
I beat myself up in my head for not working out enough times this week. The experience of recording my spend was… fine? I do this mentally with expenses anyway, so it wasn’t eye-opening or anything. I can’t see myself changing anything with regards to spend in the near future.

Money Diaries are meant to reflect an individual’s experience and do not necessarily reflect Refinery29’s point of view. Refinery29 in no way encourages illegal activity or harmful behavior.

title: The Best Collabs Of The Week, From Skims & Target To Depop
text:

title: I Tried The Viral Nipple Covers All Over My Feed — & I May Never Wear A Bra Again
text:
I Tried The Viral Nipple Covers All Over My Feed — & I May Never Wear A Bra Again

In an ideal world, I’d never wear a strapless bra again. No hate to them, but with summer finally here, I can’t think of a more unappealing undergarment when it comes to tiny-tank-top-and-strappy sundress season — the marks that it leaves on the hot skin, the constricting material, the underboob sweat marks, the constant slipping… As if my phone was listening to my innermost thoughts (I’m not convinced that it isn’t, for the record), my social feeds started to get flooded with ads for Cakes, a brand of nipple covers that has intrigued me since first making rounds on TikTok over a year ago.

After first becoming popular for its Grippy Cakes, adhesive-free nipple covers, the brand has more recently unveiled the heat wave-friendly Sticky Cakes, which have a tacky adhesive layer to offer more support (and peace of mind). Cakes’ nipple covers come in a few different sizes (“itty bitty” for AAA-A cups, “OG” for B-DD cups, and “+” for DDD cups and up), skin tones (Honey, Caramel, and Cocoa), and shapes (circles and triangles).

I’ve had mixed success with nipple covers in the past. While the objective is to create a smooth surface underneath tight and/or sheer clothing, some of them made my breast outline even more pronounced as a result of thicker material or uneven edges, defeating the point entirely. Others made an early exit (this happened during my wedding reception, and I didn’t realize until the after-party — oops!) and fell off.

So, I set out to find out if Cakes, with their $33 price point — which hovers just above many of its competitors — were the real deal. (Although they are 30% off right now, BTW.) From white tees to bikini tops (yes, bikini tops!) to backless dresses, I put Cakes Grippy Circles, Grippy Triangles, Sticky Circles, and Sticky Triangles, all in the “OG” size and Honey colorway, to the test. Ahead, my thoughts.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Grippy Cakes Circles, $33 $23.10

First up, I tried the Grippy Cakes Circles. The silicone was smooth and soft, with a contoured shape that was thickest in the center and gradually thinned out towards the edges. As with any nipple covers, I applied them to clean, dry skin. I probably could’ve sized down in the circles because they nearly covered my entire breast. This is not necessarily a good or bad thing, especially considering that nipples and breasts vary in size and shape, but something to be aware of if your breasts are on the smaller side of the brand’s range.

The brand recommends wearing this style under tight clothing to help the Cakes stay in place, but I wore mine under a loosely fitting white T-shirt, and they were not only undetectable as advertised but felt secure all day, even in summer heat. After wearing them for a full day, I gently removed them, rinsed them with warm water, and patted them dry. According to the brand, if you follow these instructions, Grippy Cakes are reusable since they use your body’s heat, not adhesive, to naturally cling onto the skin. (Buying fewer, better things? Here for it.)

The circle-shaped “style” was most similar to other nipple covers I’ve tried in the past, but I found that these held up better with sweat and seamlessly blended with my skin (none of those uneven-edge issues I’ve experienced in the past). I would definitely wear these again under a sheer blouse or a plain white tee. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Grippy Cakes Triangles, $33 $23.10

Later that week, I gave the Grippy Triangles, which have an elongated, pointed shape that offers coverage for trickier styles, a try; since they have a sleeker profile, they work for low-cut or V-neck styles that the Circles may have peeked out from. What’s more, Cakes says you can wear these with swimwear (and for working out, but I tend to need more significant support if I’m doing anything more intense than walking). To test this theory, I threw on a triangle bikini and hopped in the pool. I was honestly impressed that the covers stayed in place through swimming and then laying out in the sun; water and sweat didn’t affect the grippiness of the silicone whatsoever. 

Would these make it through surfing in Montauk? Probably not. But a little dip and/or playing mermaids is more than fine for these. I probably wouldn’t wear them again under swimwear because I look for styles that already have light padding in them. However, I appreciate having the option for sweat-filled days, and would recommend these for brides who want to dance the night away without worrying about a wardrobe malfunction like mine or, worse, a nip slip.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Sticky Cakes Circles & Triangles, $33 $23.10

Lastly, I tried the new Sticky Cakes, which are nearly identical to their grippy counterparts in look and feel (they come in the same silicone material) but are coated in a thin layer of medical-grade adhesive. Sticky-front bras have been in my wardrobe arsenal for years now, providing light support and lift in backless, strapless designs. But I’m always on the hunt for something better, whether that’s in terms of comfort, performance, or both. (Cakes just released their version, called the Cleavage Bra, which I am eager to try.) 

Sticky Cakes are a nice middle ground between going braless and the aforementioned sticky bras. The design has a small divot in the center (called a “nip nook”), so you don’t get adhesive anywhere near the delicate nipple area. When compared to Grippy Cakes, these felt more secure. The adhesive was tacky enough to stay in place (even in 90°F summer heat) but wasn’t so sticky that it hurt to remove it at the end of the day. Per the brand, the sticky versions can be worn at least 10 times with proper care and storage, which involves gently rinsing with warm water, air-drying them, and storing them in the included pouch. I would save this style for my backless summer dresses on the hottest days of the season or an outdoor summer music festival.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Final Thoughts

So, is Cakes worth the hype? I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t impressed. The grippy styles are great from a sustainability perspective. To me, the triangle shapes are a game-changer thanks to the way you can rotate them to accommodate even the trickiest neckline work. I also felt like these were the most seamless, invisible alternative to bras I’ve tried so far. Out of all the combinations I tried, the sticky triangles ended up being the winner in my book, since the shape was a universal fit for any tricky wardrobe situation, and I like having the adhesive as an insurance measure.

Bonus: The brand is dedicated to supporting women’s health via Cakes Cares, the brand’s philanthropic arm, which has donated over a million dollars to breast cancer research and support programs. (As the daughter of a breast cancer survivor, I love this.)

Now that I’ve got a full wardrobe of Cakes at my disposal, I feel that my search for the perfect nipple cover has ended. From future wedding dance floors to music festivals and other sweaty, bra-unfriendly scenarios, I may never wear bras again — or at least for the summer.

title: I Love My Job But I Make More Money From My Sugar Daddy
text:
I Love My Job But I Make More Money From My Sugar Daddy

You wouldn’t be reading this unless David*, my sugar daddy, was putting £2,000 (around $2,600) directly into my bank account every month. I’m 32 and I’ve been in a financial arrangement with David, a divorced, 52-year-old American CEO, for three years. 

I met him on Seeking, the infamous sugar daddy website where young women needing financial assistance look for older, richer men who are willing to help. Officially, there is no exchange for sexual services permitted on Seeking but I won’t mince my words: It’s an escort site. Sex and money are at the forefront of every member’s interactions. 

Before meeting David, I’d had good and bad experiences with men I met on the site. One man took me to a cheap bar for a drink and offered me £200 ($260) for sex. I declined. Another gave me £16,000 cash ($20,700) at a gas station to rent my own flat for six months because he “wanted to help” and expected nothing in return. I accepted. Both are scenarios I’m still puzzled by. But when David and I started chatting, it felt more akin to normal dating. After a week of back-and-forth messaging, we met for the first time in one of London’s stylish restaurants. My train was delayed, leaving him waiting for 30 minutes past our agreed meeting time. I panicked, hating to be late, but he reassured me that he’d wait and insisted I didn’t rush. I finally turned up and what followed was just a really great date. We spoke at length on various topics and shared details of our personal lives over cocktails, wine and three courses. There was an instant connection and I think he knew it too. Conversation flowed despite our differing political viewpoints. Sex and money were put on the back burner. I could see how and why he was successful. He was charming, gentlemanly and intelligent. His net worth was also well into seven figures. 

Our arrangement started in December 2021 and progressed slowly. We scheduled dates across Mayfair (a wealthy part of London) and with each meet we became increasingly close, physically and mentally. Cuddling up in dark, quiet corners of upmarket cocktail bars, we’d talk softly, gently hold hands and passionately kiss between conversations. I’d rub my lower leg on his shins underneath the table and act suggestively but we always made sure to show decency in public, though the sexual tension was clear. When I kissed him, I could smell his aftershave — fresh and subtle. I loved that he always made an effort. He dressed smartly, looking every bit the CEO. He’d compliment me freely, flirting with me and telling me how great I looked but teasing me about yet another all-black outfit choice. Far from arrogant and rude, he treated waiting staff exceptionally well, leaving generous tips as he surreptitiously paid the bill (he is American, after all). Each time we called it a night, he’d ask me if I needed any help, subtly slipping £200 or £500 ($650) into my hand before finding a black cab to take me home. He was in and out of London, traveling with work and back to his main home in the States, so we didn’t sleep together for over a year after our first meeting. To this day, we’ve only slept together that one time. Our schedules are tricky to align.

After three years of messaging most days and financial help when needed, I asked David for more money. I was made redundant from my permanent writing role, London was getting expensive, my rent had gone up 25% and I was worried. I was embarrassed at first — it felt awkward and uncouth — but I was surprised by how unfazed he was. Here is a man who doesn’t worry about money, is generous with his own and understanding of my situation. He’s older than me and knows the difficulties of being young and broke but has never made me feel lesser because of it. From then on, he started depositing £500 directly into my account every Thursday. At one moment, during the London leg of Taylor Swift’s tour, I told him that I’d missed out on tickets but last-minute seats were available for an extortionate amount of money. Before I knew it, £1,000 ($1,300) was in my account and I was walking into Wembley Stadium. 

I am writing this anonymously so that I can be an open book, which means it’s true when I say that all he asks for in return are nude photos of me (which I am more than happy to provide), honesty and regular communication. I’m still perplexed by this so I asked him: “Why do you help me?” This is what he had to say: “Because I actually care about you! And there is a thrill and a mystery to us. Plus, there’s the fact I find you to be intelligent, sexy, funny and a challenge.” 

This relationship is obviously transactional but not like-for-like. David doesn’t demand pictures and I don’t demand payment. We stay in regular contact and conversation is fluid. I know what he wants and he knows what I want; an understanding and trust has formed over the years, which means we don’t need to speak constantly about the nature of the arrangement. I’m always quick to address friends’ concerns that I might feel pressure to do something I don’t want to do but David has always made it clear that under no circumstances am I to do anything I’m uncomfortable with. 

This relationship isn’t one-sided. I care a lot about him. He’s inspiring, thoughtful, kind and funny, and helps me look at life in a different way. He’s unwaveringly generous with his emotional support and money and in no way controlling. I am free to do as I please and go to him for advice, help or comfort when needed. I like to think I’m respectful of his time and money. I have managed to save a lot thanks to him and I never waste cash on frivolous material possessions (minus one designer handbag I couldn’t resist). I pay my rent and bills on time, I buy food and I’m able to visit my family thanks to him. I could easily splash the cash on more designer bags, shoes, clothes, extravagant evenings out and Ubers but I’m mature enough to realize how fortunate I am to be in this position. Am I also cheekily trying to persuade him to buy me a flat of my own? Yes, but you can’t blame a girl for trying. 

The crux of this arrangement is that I’m at an age where I have limited time to settle down and have children. I can’t afford to keep myself as a freelance journalist and I want to stay living in London. I could also be approaching a time where I’m no longer desirable to David. It might sound problematic but will he want to help me when I’m nearing 40? This crossroads in my life is slowly approaching. I know I need to get real, stop living in fantasy land and off someone else’s money but it’s complicated. I love this arrangement, I love money, I love my relationship with David and I don’t want it to end — but it’s unrealistic to expect it to go on forever.

Whether I can see myself ending up with David is something I occasionally think about but in all honesty, I think we both know it wouldn’t work. He’s a grandfather and I’d eventually want children. He’s American and his primary residence is in the US. We have a 20-year age gap. Logistically, it doesn’t add up. 

A handful of friends are aware of my arrangement but I keep my family in the dark. I hide this very big part of my life because of the overwhelming disapproval and judgment I know I’d receive. Of course, I am an adult and I’m aware of the perceived and very real exploitation of young women and how this is an incredibly important and contentious issue. Men are commonly seen to be taking advantage of struggling women in these kinds of relationships but my counter argument is that if it’s between two consenting adults who are happy to have this style of relationship and are communicating their needs effectively, does it hurt anyone? Is it as wrong as it’s sometimes made out to be? It goes without saying that I morally oppose any relationship of this kind where this isn’t the case. 

I am working hard to become financially independent as a journalist. I’m applying for full-time jobs and regularly pitching ideas to editors but if the time comes where I can’t make ends meet within this career choice or David decides to end the arrangement, I am willing to consider alternative employment and living circumstances. And while I’m not actively dating in the traditional sense, I would also consider ending the arrangement if the right man came along. In the three years I’ve known David, a handful of men my own age have asked me out — all on mediocre, unappealing dates. One asked me to come to his house to watch Netflix on the first date because he “couldn’t be bothered to take me for dinner.” One expected me to travel to a bar over an hour’s train ride away (and a five-minute walk from his flat) and one ghosted me after arranging drinks. I’m not against dating men my own age but, in my experience, older men tend to be far more gentlemanly and considerate, often meeting me halfway between our homes or insisting on dinner dates and getting me an Uber home so I’m safe. The chivalry is unmatched and while it might make me sound like a princess, I can’t help but find it incredibly attractive. 

I sought David’s permission to write this feature and while he wasn’t keen on the idea, I felt it was worthwhile to provide another viewpoint on sugar daddy relationships. Not all are problematic nor (forgive me) tit for tat; they can be respectful, honest and mutually beneficial.

*Name has been changed to protect identity

This article was published in October 2024 and has since been updated.
